idiom_name: struct CowBuf { _Atomic size_t refs; size_t len; char *data; } + clone-before-write helper
implementation_notes: C has no copy constructors, destructors or ownership annotations, so the whole handle/body structure is written by hand: a struct holding a pointer to the heap body and a reference count, a cow_write() helper that checks the count and clones the body before the first modification, and an explicit cow_release() that decrements and frees at zero. C11 <stdatomic.h> supplies the count primitives (atomic_fetch_add/atomic_fetch_sub with explicit memory orders), or a plain size_t suffices while the value stays inside one thread. Nothing replaces the classic structure here - it is the only realization - so reserve it for genuinely large buffers; for small values the count and the branch cost more than the memcpy they avoid.
pitfalls: A non-atomic count races: two threads can both clone, or both write the supposedly private body; use atomic_fetch_add/atomic_fetch_sub or keep the value thread-confined, which is the cheaper answer.
cow_release() must run on every error path - C has no destructor, so a missed release leaks the body and a double release corrupts the allocator.
memcpy'ing the handle struct instead of calling an explicit cow_clone() creates two owners of one count, and the body is freed twice.
Cloning shallowly (copying only the outer struct) leaves nested buffers shared after a write that was supposed to be private.
